blocks.text: A man with a failing heart presses a thumb into his shin and leaves a dent that takes seconds to fill. A woman with nephrotic syndrome wakes with puffy eyelids. A patient with a blocked renal artery has a wedge of dead, pale kidney. Fluid in the wrong place and tissue deprived of blood are two faces of the same subject: how the circulation delivers, exchanges and fails.

blocks.markdown: **Oedema** is an excess of fluid in the interstitial space (or in body cavities, when it is called effusion, for example ascites or pleural effusion). **Congestion** is the passive accumulation of blood in a tissue because of impaired venous outflow. **Infarction** is ischaemic necrosis caused by occlusion of the arterial supply or, less commonly, of the venous drainage.

blocks.title: Starling forces
blocks.text: Fluid movement across the capillary wall depends on a balance between hydrostatic pressures (which push fluid out) and oncotic pressures (which draw fluid in, driven mainly by plasma albumin). At the arteriolar end, outward hydrostatic force exceeds inward oncotic force, so fluid leaves; at the venular end, the oncotic force predominates, so fluid returns. Lymphatics drain the small net excess.

blocks.caption: P_c is capillary hydrostatic pressure, P_i interstitial hydrostatic pressure, pi_c plasma oncotic pressure and pi_i interstitial oncotic pressure, all in mmHg. A positive value means net filtration out of the capillary.

rows: Impaired venous return or fluid retention
Heart failure; deep vein thrombosis; venous obstruction; salt and water retention in renal disease
Hypoalbuminaemia from loss or reduced synthesis
Nephrotic syndrome; cirrhosis; protein-losing enteropathy; malnutrition
Tumour infiltration, surgery or radiation, filariasis
Renal retention of salt and water
blocks.caption: Pathophysiological mechanisms of oedema.

blocks.title: Applying Starling forces
blocks.prompt: In a patient with right heart failure, capillary hydrostatic pressure rises to 35 mmHg. Take plasma oncotic pressure 25 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure 2 mmHg and interstitial oncotic pressure 5 mmHg. Calculate the net filtration pressure and interpret it.

steps.text: Write the equation: net = (Pc - Pi) - (pi_c - pi_i).
Net: 33 - 20 = +13 mmHg, a strongly positive outward pressure that exceeds lymphatic capacity.

blocks.answer: +13 mmHg: net filtration, so fluid accumulates as oedema.

blocks.markdown: Oedema is **pitting** if a finger impression remains (typical of cardiac or hypoalbuminaemic oedema), and is often dependent (legs when upright, sacrum when supine). Pulmonary oedema impairs gas exchange; cerebral oedema raises intracranial pressure and can lead to herniation. Sodium and water retention occurs in heart failure partly through reduced renal perfusion and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

### Chronic passive congestion of the liver

Right heart failure causes increased pressure in the hepatic veins. Blood backs up into the sinusoids around the **central veins**, which become congested and dark red, and the centrilobular hepatocytes become hypoxic and may undergo necrosis. Periportal hepatocytes receive better-oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and are preserved, producing the **nutmeg liver** appearance: a dark red congested centrilobular pattern alternating with paler periportal tissue, resembling a cut nutmeg. With long-standing congestion, fibrosis may develop around central veins (**cardiac cirrhosis**). Left heart failure causes chronic pulmonary congestion with haemosiderin-laden macrophages ('heart failure cells'). In both cases the cells nearest the venous end suffer the most hypoxia.

### Infarction

Most infarcts follow **arterial thrombosis or embolism**. The outcome depends on the nature of the blood supply, the rate of occlusion, tissue vulnerability to hypoxia and the oxygen content of blood.

**Pale (white) infarcts** occur with arterial occlusion in **solid organs with a single (end-arterial) blood supply** and dense tissue that limits blood seepage, such as the heart, spleen and kidney.

**Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts** occur (1) with venous occlusion (for example testicular torsion, ovarian torsion), (2) in **loose tissues** where blood can collect (lung), (3) in tissues with **dual circulation or rich collateral supply** (lung, small intestine) where blood from the other supply seeps into the dead tissue, (4) in tissues previously congested, and (5) when flow is re-established after necrosis. Most infarcts are wedge-shaped, with the apex pointing to the occluded vessel and the base at the organ surface.

rows: Venous occlusion, or arterial occlusion in loose or dual-supply tissue
Loose or dual-supply tissue; congested tissue
blocks.caption: Pale and red infarcts.

blocks.title: Classify the infarct
blocks.prompt: (a) A 30-year-old man develops a dark, swollen testis after torsion of the spermatic cord. (b) A patient with atrial fibrillation has a wedge-shaped, pale yellow lesion in the spleen. Classify each infarct and explain why.

steps.text: (a) Torsion twists the cord and first occludes the thin-walled veins, while arterial inflow continues. Blood enters but cannot leave, so the tissue becomes engorged and haemorrhagic: red infarct due to venous occlusion.
(b) The spleen is a solid organ with an end-arterial supply; an embolus from the heart occludes the splenic artery branch and there is no collateral flow to seep blood: pale infarct.

blocks.answer: (a) Red infarct (venous occlusion); (b) pale infarct (arterial occlusion in a solid end-arterial organ).

items: Pitting oedema is typical of cardiac oedema and hypoalbuminaemia.
Nutmeg liver is caused by chronic passive congestion, typically from right-sided heart failure.
Infarcts are usually wedge-shaped, and the brain shows liquefactive necrosis.
Pulmonary infarcts are typically red and wedge-shaped, occurring in congested or dual-supply lungs.

blocks.title: Why centrilobular?
blocks.text: In passive hepatic congestion the zone around the central vein is most affected because it is the furthest from the oxygenated hepatic artery and portal blood, and it lies at the point where venous back-pressure is transmitted.

points: Starling forces (hydrostatic and oncotic pressures) govern fluid movement; oedema arises from raised hydrostatic pressure, reduced oncotic pressure, increased permeability, lymphatic obstruction or sodium retention.
Pale infarcts follow arterial occlusion in solid end-arterial organs; red infarcts follow venous occlusion or occur in loose or dual-supply tissue.
Chronic passive hepatic congestion produces a nutmeg liver, with congested, hypoxic centrilobular zones.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of generalised oedema in nephrotic syndrome?

options.text: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from loss of albumin in urine
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from right heart failure
Lymphatic obstruction by tumour
Increased vascular permeability from acute inflammation

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from loss of albumin in urine
questions.explanation: Heavy proteinuria lowers plasma albumin and so oncotic pressure, reducing the force that draws fluid back into capillaries. The result is generalised oedema, often visible around the eyes.

questions.stem: A woman develops unilateral swelling of the leg after a deep vein thrombosis of the femoral vein. Which Starling force is mainly altered?

options.text: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
Decreased interstitial oncotic pressure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: venous obstruction raises back-pressure in the capillaries.
distractorRationale.b: Plasma albumin is normal in this setting.
distractorRationale.c: Interstitial pressure rises as a consequence.
distractorRationale.d: Interstitial oncotic pressure is not primarily altered.

questions.explanation: A thrombus obstructs venous outflow, raising pressure within downstream capillaries and so favouring filtration. The oedema is localised to the affected limb.

questions.stem: At autopsy a liver is dark red with pale mottling that looks like a cut nutmeg. The patient had long-standing right heart failure. Which zone of the lobule is congested and dark?

options.text: Centrilobular zone around the central vein
Periportal zone
Capsule only
Bile ducts

questions.correctOptionText: Centrilobular zone around the central vein

distractorRationale.b: Periportal zones are better oxygenated and are the pale areas.
distractorRationale.d: Bile ducts are not the congested element.

questions.explanation: Raised hepatic venous pressure congests the sinusoids around central veins and makes centrilobular hepatocytes hypoxic. The better-perfused periportal zone remains paler.

questions.stem: A patient with a left atrial thrombus embolises to the kidney. Which infarct type is expected, and why?

options.text: Pale infarct, because the kidney is a solid organ with an end-arterial supply
Red infarct, because the kidney has a dual blood supply
Red infarct, because the kidney is loose tissue
Pale infarct, because veins are occluded

questions.correctOptionText: Pale infarct, because the kidney is a solid organ with an end-arterial supply

distractorRationale.b: The kidney does not have a dual supply.

questions.explanation: Arterial occlusion of a dense organ with end-arterial supply gives little haemorrhage into the necrotic tissue, so the infarct is pale and wedge-shaped.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic left heart failure has a lung infarct after a pulmonary embolus. Why is it likely to be red rather than pale?

options.text: Loose lung tissue, a dual blood supply and pre-existing congestion allow haemorrhage into dead tissue
Lung tissue is rich in collagen that resists bleeding
The pulmonary artery supplies no blood to the lung
Venous occlusion is always the cause

questions.correctOptionText: Loose lung tissue, a dual blood supply and pre-existing congestion allow haemorrhage into dead tissue

distractorRationale.b: The lung is spongy, not collagen-dense.
distractorRationale.c: The pulmonary artery supplies deoxygenated blood to the lung.
distractorRationale.d: The cause is arterial, but tissue characteristics allow bleeding.

questions.explanation: Pulmonary infarcts are red because loose tissue lets blood accumulate, the bronchial arteries provide a second supply that bleeds into the area, and congestion from heart failure adds pressure. Dense end-arterial organs by contrast produce pale infarcts.

questions.stem: True or false: Nutmeg liver results from chronic passive congestion.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Raised hepatic venous pressure causes centrilobular congestion alternating with paler periportal tissue. This gives the nutmeg pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has capillary hydrostatic pressure 20 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure 1 mmHg, plasma oncotic pressure 14 mmHg and interstitial oncotic pressure 4 mmHg. Calculate the net filtration pressure in mmHg (positive means outward).
questions.explanation: Net = (20 - 1) - (14 - 4) = 19 - 10 = +9 mmHg. The low plasma oncotic pressure from reduced albumin synthesis makes net filtration strongly positive, causing oedema and ascites.

questions.stem: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, capillary hydrostatic pressure is 25 mmHg, interstitial hydrostatic pressure 0 mmHg and interstitial oncotic pressure 3 mmHg. Plasma oncotic pressure has fallen so that net filtration pressure is +14 mmHg. Calculate the plasma oncotic pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Rearranging, 14 = (25 - 0) - (pi_c - 3), so pi_c - 3 = 11 and pi_c = 14 mmHg. This is lower than the typical normal plasma oncotic pressure used in teaching, consistent with hypoalbuminaemia.

questions.stem: Explain the pathological changes of chronic passive congestion of the liver from right heart failure, including the gross appearance.
markingGuide: Raised hepatic venous pressure transmitted to sinusoids around central veins
Centrilobular congestion and hypoxia with necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes
Periportal zone preserved (better oxygenation via hepatic artery)
Nutmeg appearance (dark red mottled with pale)
questions.explanation: The pathology follows the venous back-pressure and the oxygen gradient across the lobule. Chronic injury can end in fibrosis.

questions.stem: Distinguish red from pale infarcts by mechanism and tissue type, and classify infarction of the small intestine from volvulus.
markingGuide: Pale: arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial supply (heart, spleen, kidney)
Red: venous occlusion, or loose tissue, dual circulation or congestion
Small intestine volvulus: venous occlusion first, loose tissue and rich collateral supply: red (haemorrhagic) infarct
Explanation of seepage of blood into dead tissue
questions.explanation: Pale infarcts occur where blood cannot seep into dense necrotic tissue. Torsion or volvulus obstructs veins first, which leads to engorgement and a red infarct.
